The origin of the Chicago-style hot dog is a matter of conflicting accounts. According to d4 (Wikipedia) and d8 (UChicago Voices), the Chicago-style hot dog first debuted at the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago, where two Austro-Hungarian immigrants sold Vienna Beef franks, and the style grew from there as a reflection of the city's diverse immigrant communities. By contrast, d1 and d5 argue that the Chicago-style hot dog as we know it truly originated during the Great Depression, when Fluky's (founded 1929) sold the first "Depression Sandwich" — a frankfurter topped with mustard, pickle relish, onions, a dill pickle, hot peppers, lettuce, and tomatoes for a nickel — making it an affordable meal for working-class Chicagoans [d1][d5]. Meanwhile, d7 (Britannica) and d3 trace the underlying sausage's roots further back to German immigrants who brought frankfurters to New York in the 1860s, with the first hot dog stand opened on Coney Island in 1871 by Charles Feltman, before the style spread to Chicago [d7][d3]. Adding another layer, d8 notes that each topping of the Chicago-style hot dog reflects a distinct immigrant group — German, Jewish, Polish, Italian, Greek, and Southern American — suggesting the style evolved gradually rather than having a single point of origin [d8].
